content: H5N2 is a subtype of the avian influenza virus, scientifically classified as Influenzavirus A. This virus has been associated with several outbreaks of avian influenza, some of which have had significant economic and agricultural consequences. In 1983, a highly pathogenic strain of H5N2 caused widespread outbreaks in Pennsylvania, USA, affecting chickens and turkeys and leading to substantial economic losses. Similarly, in 1994, an outbreak in Mexico impacted chickens, and a smaller outbreak occurred in Italy in 1997, also affecting chickens. On November 12, 2005, it was reported that two birds in Kuwait were infected with avian influenza. One of these birds, a migrating flamingo found on a beach, was infected with the H5N1 strain, while the other, an imported falcon, was found to carry the milder H5N2 strain. In China, an inactivated form of the H5N2 virus has been utilized as a vaccine to protect against the H5N1 strain. On May 11, 2006, Japan's Health Ministry reported that 93 poultry farm workers near Tokyo might have been exposed to the H5N2 virus in 2005. This was notable because H5N2 was not previously known to infect humans. However, none of the individuals tested positive for the virus itself, nor did they develop any flu-like symptoms. Following H5N2 outbreaks in the Ibaraki region, approximately 5.7 million birds were culled to contain the spread of the virus. In 2006, an outbreak of H5N2 occurred on a single farm in South Africa, leading to the culling of all 60 ostriches on the farm. The strain involved in this outbreak was similar to one that had caused outbreaks in South Africa during 2004 and 2005. In 2007, a low-pathogenic strain of H5N2 was detected during routine testing of 25,000 turkeys in Pendleton County, West Virginia, prior to their slaughter. Later in 2007, on December 21, an H5N2 outbreak was identified in the Dominican Republic, specifically in a suburb of Higuey City on the eastern side of the island. Although the infected birds—15 roosters and 2 hens—showed no visible signs of infection, they were culled to prevent further spread of the virus.
